title: Short Stuff: Semantic Satiation
summary: Short Stuff episode on semantic satiation, the phenomenon where repeating or staring at a word makes it lose its meaning and sound or look strange. The hosts cover the 1907 American Journal of Psychology description, Leon James coining the term in 1962 at the University of Hawaii, and related reactive inhibition (such as nose blindness to household smells). They discuss how the effect applies to music charts and burnout on songs (Journey's "Don't Stop Believing" comes up as an example), how words carry emotional associations and can prime emotions like anger, and James's experiment calling people who stutter, which reportedly reduced their stuttering over time. The episode closes with the hosts linking this to exposure therapy for fears such as flying.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to semantic satiation
segments.summary: Josh introduces the idea that a word repeated many times starts to sound or look strange and falls apart into sounds or letters, and names this semantic satiation.

segments.title: 1907 description and experience of seeing words
segments.summary: The hosts read the 1907 American Journal of Psychology description of a printed word becoming foreign and meaningless when viewed steadily. They note the loss of familiarity is subjective and can happen from looking as well as writing.

segments.title: Leon James, terminology, and neural fatigue
segments.summary: Leon James, a University of Hawaii psychology professor, coined the term semantic satiation in 1962 and listed other names for it. He described it as fatigue, comparing it to neurons that respond less on repeated firing, with the brain conserving energy.

segments.title: Reactive inhibition and nose blindness
segments.summary: Semantic satiation is described as a type of reactive inhibition, the same process behind becoming nose blind to household smells.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Music charts and song burnout
segments.summary: Leon James found that songs that rise quickly up the charts also fade quickly, while slower climbers fade slowly. The hosts tie this to burnout on songs, using Journey's Don't Stop Believing as an example, and note that songs can return after a break.

segments.title: Words as emotion and music
segments.summary: Repetition can make lyrics feel like musical notes rather than words, using Steve Perry as an example. The hosts also discuss how words can prime emotions such as anger.

segments.title: Stuttering experiment and exposure
segments.summary: James reportedly called people who stutter repeatedly and found they stuttered less over time. The hosts compare this to exposure, such as fear of flying lessening with repeated flights.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and the show credits iHeartRadio.
